Main.sentence: The Congressional Budget Office ( CBO ) is a ___E:federal agency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_federal_agencies)___ within the ___E:legislative branch U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress)___ of the ___E:United States government U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_government)___ that provides budget and economic information to Congress.

Inspired by California's ___E:Legislative Analyst's Office U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Legislative_Analyst%27s_Office)___ that manages the state budget in a strictly nonpartisan fashion, the CBO was created as a nonpartisan agency by the ___E:Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act of 1974 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Budget_and_Impoundment_Control_Act_of_1974)___ .

Whereas politicians on both sides of the aisle have criticized the CBO when its estimates have been politically inconvenient,   economists and other academics overwhelmingly reject that the CBO is partisan or that it fails to produce credible forecasts.

There is a consensus among economists that "adjusting for legal restrictions on what the CBO can assume about future legislation and events, the CBO has historically issued credible forecasts of the effects of both Democratic and Republican legislative proposals."

The Congressional Budget Office was created by Title II of the ___E:Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act of 1974 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Budget_and_Impoundment_Control_Act_of_1974)___ (Pub. L. 93-344), which was signed into law by President ___E:Richard Nixon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Nixon)___ on July 12, 1974.  Official operations began on February 24, 1975, with ___E:Alice Rivlin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Rivlin)___ as director.

The CBO's creation stems from a fight between President Nixon and a ___E:Democratic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States))___ -controlled ___E:Congress U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress)___ .
Congress wanted to protect its ___E:power of the purse U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_of_the_purse)___ from the executive.

The CBO was created "within the legislative branch to bolster Congress's budgetary understanding and ability to act. Lawmakers' aim was both technical and political: Generate a source of budgetary expertise to aid in writing annual budgets and lessen the legislature's reliance on the president's ___E:Office of Management and Budget U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_Management_and_Budget)___ ."  In 2015, the Brookings Institution reported that since its creation, the CBO has since supplanted the OMB "as the authoritative source of information on the economy and the budget in the eyes of Congress, the press, and the public."

The Congressional Budget Office is ___E:nonpartisan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonpartisanism)___ , and produces "independent analyses of budgetary and economic issues to support the Congressional budget process."  Each year, the agency releases reports and cost estimates for proposed legislation, without issuing any policy recommendations.

With respect to estimating spending for Congress, the Congressional Budget Office serves a purpose parallel to that of the ___E:Joint Committee on Taxation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Congress_Joint_Committee_on_Taxation)___ for estimating revenue for Congress, the ___E:Department of the Treasury U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_the_Treasury)___ for estimating revenues for the ___E:Executive branch U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_(government))___ .
This includes projections on the effect on ___E:national debt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_debt)___ and cost estimates for legislation.

Section 202(e) of the Budget Act requires the CBO to submit periodic reports about fiscal policy to the ___E:House U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_Committee_on_the_Budget)___ and ___E:Senate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_the_Budget)___ budget committees to provide baseline projections of the federal budget.
This is currently done by preparation of an annual Economic and Budget Outlook plus a mid-year update.

The agency also each year issues An Analysis of the President's Budgetary Proposals for the upcoming fiscal year per a standing request of the ___E:Senate Committee on Appropriations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_Committee_on_Appropriations)___ .

These three series are designated essential titles distributed to ___E:Federal Depository Libraries U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_depository_library)___ and are available for purchase from the ___E:Government Publishing Office U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Government_Publishing_Office)___ .
The CBO often provides testimony in response to requests from various Congressional committees and issues letters responding to queries made by members of Congress.
The Congressional Budget Office is divided into nine divisions.

The ___E:Speaker of the House of Representatives U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaker_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives)___ and the ___E:President pro tempore of the Senate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_pro_tempore_of_the_United_States_Senate)___ jointly appoint the CBO Director after considering recommendations from the two budget committees.
The term of office is four years, with no limit on the number of terms a director may serve.
Either house of Congress, however, may remove the director by resolution.
At the expiration of a term of office, the person serving as Director may continue in the position until his or her successor is appointed.

Whereas politicians on both sides of the aisle have criticized the CBO when its estimates have been politically inconvenient,   economists and other academics overwhelmingly reject that the CBO is partisan or that it fails to produce credible forecasts.

A March 2017 survey of leading economists shows a consensus behind the notion that "adjusting for legal restrictions on what the CBO can assume about future legislation and events, the CBO has historically issued credible forecasts of the effects of both Democratic and Republican legislative proposals."  According to MIT economist ___E:David Autor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Autor)___ , the "CBO has a good track record with a very difficult assignment.

It errs, but not systematically or with partisan intent."  According to Yale economist ___E:Christopher Udry U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Udry)___ , "There is no credible evidence of partisan bias."  Economist ___E:Walter E. Williams U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_E._Williams)___ , a ___E:classical liberal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_liberal)___ , wrote in 1998 that the CBO was well-regarded for its "honest numbers" on fiscal and economic matters.

According to the Los Angeles Times , "the CBO's analyses and forecasting are regarded as good or better than others doing similar work... economists say that the CBO's economic projections generally compare favorably against other outfits, and its long-term budget estimates have been fairly accurate."

According to George Washington University political scientist Sarah Binder, the CBO "has emerged over its history as a neutral analyst of congressional budgets and cost estimates for proposed legislation."  The agency has "a nonpartisan staff culture".

Historically, the ___E:House Budget Committee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_Budget_Committee)___ and ___E:Senate Budget Committee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_Budget_Committee)___ have insulated the CBO from external pressures and attempts to politicize or weaken the office.
Professor Philip Joyce of the ___E:University of Maryland School of Public Policy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Maryland_School_of_Public_Policy)___ writes:
This is quite surprising, in a sense, given the partisan nature of the Congress.
It is not necessarily that these partisans have embraced nonpartisanship as a positive end in itself, however.

Rather, the Budget Committees (and especially their leadership and staff) have recognized that a weak CBO (one that does not have a reputation for objective analysis, and whose conclusions are viewed as partisan) is not in their interest.
A weak CBO weakens the Budget Committees, and indeed weakens Congress as a whole in its inevitable battles with the executive over budget and economic policy.
